title: What prompt characteristic most improves the likelihood of receiving a response that matches the user's expectations?
feedback:
High-quality prompts clearly communicate the objective, provide sufficient context, and define the expected outcome. These elements help the model generate responses that are relevant, accurate, and easier to use. Provide clear, specific instructions with context.
Source
answer1: Clearly defining the objective, context, and desired outcome.
explanation1: Explicit objectives, relevant context, and a defined outcome reduce ambiguity and guide the model toward the intended response.
answer2: Using broad questions that allow the model to determine the objective.
explanation2: Broad questions increase ambiguity and make responses less predictable.
answer3: Adding as much information as possible, even if it is unrelated.
explanation3: Irrelevant information can distract the model from the user's real objective.
answer4: Avoiding constraints so the model can respond more creatively.
explanation4: Removing constraints often reduces consistency and increases output variability.

title: What is the primary weakness of zero-shot prompting when a Scrum Team expects a very specific output structure?
feedback:
Zero-shot prompting can be useful for simple tasks, but it becomes weaker when the expected format is specific and has not been demonstrated. Zero-shot prompting relies on internal training knowledge and cannot infer team-specific formats.
Source
answer1: The model may not infer the team's expected format without examples.
explanation1: Zero-shot prompting provides no examples, so the model must infer the structure from instructions alone.
answer2: It requires the model to be retrained before every request.
explanation2: Zero-shot prompting does not require retraining the model.
answer3: It prevents the use of clear instructions in the prompt.
explanation3: Zero-shot prompting can still include clear instructions.
answer4: It only works when the task is unrelated to Scrum.
explanation4: Zero-shot prompting can be used for Scrum-related tasks, but it may lack team-specific precision.

title: The Developers start using AI-generated test cases without changing the Definition of Done. What should the Scrum Team do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Team understands that AI-assisted testing must still support transparency and product quality. AI may help create tests, but the team remains responsible for ensuring that the Increment meets the Definition of Done. The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.
Source
answer1: Inspect whether the Definition of Done should include human review, AI traceability, and relevant quality checks.
explanation1: The team should make the impact of AI transparent and ensure the Increment still meets agreed quality expectations.
answer2: Accept AI-generated tests as sufficient when they pass automatically.
explanation2: Passing AI-generated tests alone does not prove the Increment meets the Definition of Done.
answer3: Allow the AI tool to decide when the Increment is Done.
explanation3: AI can assist, but it cannot take accountability for the Increment or the Definition of Done.
answer4: Avoid discussing the change until defects appear in production.
explanation4: Waiting for production issues weakens transparency and inspection.

title: Which set best represents key ethical concerns when using AI in an organization?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can distinguish broad ethical AI risks from technical or operational concerns. Ethical AI requires attention to fairness, privacy, transparency, explainability, and accountability. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Bias, privacy, transparency, explainability, and accountability.
explanation1: These concerns cover fairness, responsible data use, understandable outputs, and responsibility for harm.
answer2: Latency, interface design, model size, and storage cost.
explanation2: These are technical or operational concerns, not the broadest ethical concerns.
answer3: Automation speed, output length, prompt style, and formatting quality.
explanation3: These affect usability but do not represent the main ethical risk areas.
answer4: Vendor pricing, licensing terms, deployment time, and user training.
explanation4: These may matter for adoption, but they do not capture the core ethical issues of AI.

title: You are preparing a workshop with stakeholders who have conflicting views. What is the most effective and responsible way to use AI?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master understands AI as facilitation support, not as a replacement for human judgment or stakeholder participation. Responsible use means using AI to prepare options while safeguarding the purpose and psychological safety of the workshop. I'm facilitating a cross-cultural session—what icebreakers promote psychological safety?
Source
answer1: Use AI to explore facilitation options while you remain accountable for purpose, inclusion, and psychological safety.
explanation1: AI can support preparation, but the Scrum Master must preserve human facilitation, trust, and responsible participation.
answer2: Let AI select the final decision to reduce stakeholder conflict.
explanation2: AI should not replace stakeholder discussion or human accountability for decisions.
answer3: Replace difficult stakeholders with AI-generated personas to avoid tension.
explanation3: Simulated personas cannot replace real stakeholder participation and may weaken transparency.
answer4: Use AI to monitor every participant and privately score their contribution.
explanation4: Surveillance-style use can damage trust and psychological safety.

title: Team morale decreases after an AI tool starts ranking Developers by individual productivity. What should the Scrum Master do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master treats AI productivity metrics as something to inspect through the lens of trust, collaboration, and team effectiveness. Individual AI ranking can undermine Scrum if it weakens self-management or creates fear. the antithesis of the Scrum environment
Source
answer1: Facilitate a team conversation to inspect the tool's impact on trust, collaboration, and self-management.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should help the Scrum Team inspect how the AI tool affects the team system and adapt its use responsibly.
answer2: Encourage Developers to improve their individual ranking to restore confidence.
explanation2: This reinforces individual competition and does not address trust or collaboration concerns.
answer3: Ask management to use the ranking only during performance reviews.
explanation3: This keeps the harmful dynamic and shifts the issue outside the Scrum Team's inspection.
answer4: Remove every AI tool immediately and prohibit future experiments.
explanation4: A blanket ban may ignore useful AI applications, the team should inspect and adapt responsibly.

title: Which statement best explains why Artificial General Intelligence has not yet been achieved?
feedback:
This question tests the difference between powerful AI systems and true AGI. A model may perform impressive tasks, but AGI would require general capability across intellectual domains, not only narrow or trained patterns. any intellectual task
Source
answer1: Current AI systems do not reliably generalize and reason across unrelated domains like humans.
explanation1: AGI implies broad, flexible capability across intellectual tasks, while current systems remain limited and task-bounded.
answer2: AGI has not been achieved because AI systems cannot process natural language.
explanation2: Many current systems can process natural language, but that does not make them generally intelligent.
answer3: AGI has already been achieved when an LLM can answer questions fluently.
explanation3: Fluent language output is not the same as broad human-level general intelligence.
answer4: AGI only requires storing enough examples of every possible human task.
explanation4: AGI is not merely a storage problem, it requires broad transfer and reasoning across domains.

title: What practice best improves consistency when a Scrum Team shares prompts for retrospectives?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that prompt consistency comes from reusable structures, not from copying one-off prompts. A shared library with placeholders helps the Scrum Team reuse prompts while adapting them to each retrospective. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Use reusable prompt templates with clear placeholders for team-specific context.
explanation1: Templates with placeholders create a repeatable structure while allowing the team to adapt the prompt to each situation.
answer2: Let each team member create prompts independently to preserve personal style.
explanation2: Independent prompting may increase variation and reduce consistency across the team.
answer3: Copy the longest previous prompt for every retrospective.
explanation3: A long prompt is not necessarily reusable or relevant to a new context.
answer4: Store only the AI-generated outputs instead of the prompts.
explanation4: Outputs may be useful, but they do not help the team reproduce the prompting approach consistently.

title: A Scrum Team wants to upload all Sprint Retrospective recordings into an AI tool for future analysis. What is the most appropriate policy?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that AI use involving meeting data requires responsible data governance. The safest policy is to define why the data is collected, obtain informed consent, minimize sensitive information, and limit retention. Responsible & Ethical AI
Source
answer1: Define a clear purpose, obtain informed consent, minimize sensitive data, and set a retention period.
explanation1: This approach limits unnecessary data exposure and ensures the team uses AI in a responsible and transparent way.
answer2: Store all recordings indefinitely because they may be useful for future team analysis.
explanation2: Indefinite storage increases privacy risk and does not respect data minimization or purpose limitation.
answer3: Allow the AI vendor to decide which recordings should be retained.
explanation3: The Scrum Team and organization remain responsible for data governance and cannot delegate the policy entirely to the vendor.
answer4: Remove participant names after uploading the recordings to reduce privacy concerns.
explanation4: Anonymizing after upload is too late and does not address consent, purpose, or retention.

title: An AI tool suggests assigning Sprint Backlog items to Developers based on past performance data. What is the most important concern to raise?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner recognizes that AI should support the Scrum Team rather than replace its ability to manage its own work. An AI assignment tool can look efficient while weakening team ownership, collaboration, and shared accountability. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: The tool may undermine the Scrum Team's self-management by deciding who does what work.
explanation1: The main risk is that the tool shifts work ownership away from the Developers and weakens their ability to manage their own work.
answer2: The tool may require too much configuration before Sprint Planning.
explanation2: Configuration effort may matter, but it is not the most important Scrum concern.
answer3: The Product Owner may disagree with the AI's technical assignment logic.
explanation3: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog but does not assign Sprint Backlog work to Developers.
answer4: The AI may produce assignments faster than the team can review them.
explanation4: Review speed is secondary to the risk of removing self-management.

title: When a Scrum Team asks AI to support root-cause analysis, what prompting approach is most appropriate?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can select a prompting method for analytical work. For root-cause analysis, asking the model to reason step by step is more appropriate than increasing creativity or relying only on generic instructions. Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
Source
answer1: Ask the model to break the problem down step by step before giving a conclusion.
explanation1: This encourages structured reasoning and helps the team inspect the logic behind the response.
answer2: Increase randomness so the model explores more creative causes.
explanation2: Higher randomness may generate variety but can reduce analytical precision.
answer3: Use a persona prompt to permanently improve the model's reasoning ability.
explanation3: A persona can shape style or perspective, but it does not retrain the model.
answer4: Use zero-shot prompting and rely only on the model's general knowledge.
explanation4: Zero-shot prompting may be useful, but it is less suited when careful reasoning is needed.

title: A realistic AI-generated video of a company leader announces a false policy change. What is the most appropriate response?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner recognizes synthetic media as an ethical and security risk. The responsible response is to verify authenticity, limit harm, and communicate transparently rather than amplifying or ignoring the content. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Verify the video's authenticity through trusted channels and communicate the findings transparently.
explanation1: This response addresses the risk of synthetic misinformation while preserving trust and accountability.
answer2: Share the video widely so employees can decide for themselves whether it is real.
explanation2: Wider circulation may amplify misinformation and increase confusion.
answer3: Ignore the video unless employees formally complain about it.
explanation3: Ignoring a plausible deepfake can allow misinformation to spread and damage trust.
answer4: Ask AI to generate a counter-video without explaining the situation.
explanation4: A counter-video may add confusion and does not provide transparent verification.

title: A Scrum Team wants to try AI during Product Backlog refinement. What is the most responsible approach?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Team approaches AI adoption empirically. A responsible experiment should be limited, reversible, measurable, and inspected by the people affected by the change. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Run a small, reversible experiment with clear success criteria and inspect the results.
explanation1: This lets the team learn from real use while limiting risk and making the impact visible.
answer2: Replace Product Backlog refinement with AI-generated summaries for one full quarter.
explanation2: This removes important collaboration and creates too much risk before the team has learned enough.
answer3: Use AI only if it can immediately increase refinement speed.
explanation3: Speed alone does not prove the experiment improves quality, value, or shared understanding.
answer4: Let the Product Owner test AI privately and present the final process after it succeeds.
explanation4: Private experimentation reduces transparency and prevents the whole Scrum Team from learning together.

title: Does AI adoption remove the need for Scrum Master accountability?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that AI changes how some Scrum Master activities may be supported, without transferring accountability to a tool. The Scrum Master still helps the Scrum Team and organization improve their use of Scrum. Is AI Taking My Job?
Source
answer1: No, AI may assist some activities, but the Scrum Master remains accountable for enabling Scrum effectiveness.
explanation1: AI can support tasks, but it does not take over the Scrum Master's human accountability for coaching, facilitation, and helping the team improve.
answer2: Yes, because AI agents can facilitate events and resolve impediments independently.
explanation2: AI agents may assist, but they do not replace human accountability for Scrum effectiveness.
answer3: No, because AI has no impact on how Scrum Masters work.
explanation3: This is incorrect because AI can change some activities, even if accountability remains human.
answer4: Yes, because self-managing teams no longer need a Scrum Master when AI tools are available.
explanation4: AI tools do not remove the need to help teams improve their use of Scrum.

title: An AI assistant suggests several new Definition of Done items, but some do not fit the product context. What should the Scrum Team do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Team uses AI as support without outsourcing judgment. AI-generated Definition of Done items should be inspected against the product context, quality needs, and shared understanding of Done. The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.
Source
answer1: Review the suggestions together and keep only the items that improve the team's shared quality standard.
explanation1: The Scrum Team should inspect AI-generated suggestions and retain only those that support a useful and relevant Definition of Done.
answer2: Accept all suggestions because AI may identify quality gaps the team missed.
explanation2: AI may provide useful ideas, but accepting all suggestions can add irrelevant or low-value criteria.
answer3: Keep only the most innovative suggestions and discard familiar ones.
explanation3: Innovation alone does not determine whether an item belongs in the Definition of Done.
answer4: Ask the AI to decide which items are mandatory for the team.
explanation4: The Scrum Team remains responsible for its quality standard and should not delegate that judgment to AI.

title: A manager requires the Scrum Team to follow AI-generated decisions to move faster. What should the team do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Team understands that AI can assist decision-making but should not become the decision-maker. Human accountability remains essential, especially when AI recommendations affect product direction, quality, or stakeholders. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Use AI as decision support while keeping human accountability for decisions and outcomes.
explanation1: AI may support analysis, but the Scrum Team must remain responsible for the decisions it makes and the consequences that follow.
answer2: Follow the AI whenever its recommendation is faster than team discussion.
explanation2: Speed does not justify delegating accountability or bypassing human judgment.
answer3: Ask the AI vendor to approve the recommendation before the team acts.
explanation3: Vendor approval does not replace the Scrum Team's responsibility for its decisions.
answer4: Update the Definition of Done to require AI approval for all decisions.
explanation4: The Definition of Done should not be used to transfer decision accountability to AI.

title: A public AI chatbot gives plausible legal guidance without showing its sources. What is the most responsible next step?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that high-risk AI advice requires transparency, clear limits, and human oversight. A chatbot that gives plausible but risky legal guidance should not hide uncertainty or operate without visible sources. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Expose the sources, add clear legal disclaimers, and require human validation for high-risk questions.
explanation1: This protects users by improving transparency, clarifying limits, and preventing risky advice from being treated as authoritative.
answer2: Remove all uncertainty messages so users receive a clearer answer.
explanation2: Removing uncertainty creates false confidence and increases the risk of harm.
answer3: Let the chatbot decide when its answer is legally reliable.
explanation3: The chatbot should not be the sole authority for high-risk legal guidance.
answer4: Restrict the chatbot to longer explanations so the advice appears more complete.
explanation4: Longer answers can still be inaccurate, unsupported, or risky.

title: Which example best illustrates agentic AI behavior?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can distinguish agentic AI from ordinary classification, recommendation, or chatbot behavior. Agentic AI is characterized by goal-directed planning, tool use, and iterative action rather than a single isolated output. Agentic AI is the THINKING PROCESS of how to do the work, where AI systems can break down complex problems, plan, use tools, and act in a loop
Source
answer1: An AI system breaks a product research goal into tasks, uses tools, reviews outputs, and adapts its next steps.
explanation1: This shows agentic behavior because the system plans, acts, uses tools, and iterates toward a goal.
answer2: A model classifies customer comments as positive, negative, or neutral.
explanation2: Classification is a narrow task and does not show goal-directed planning or iterative tool use.
answer3: A recommendation engine suggests products based on previous purchases.
explanation3: Recommendation can be useful but does not necessarily involve autonomous planning toward a complex goal.
answer4: A chatbot answers one question using its existing training data.
explanation4: Answering a single prompt is not enough to demonstrate agentic behavior.

title: Which example best represents Artificial Narrow Intelligence?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can identify Artificial Narrow Intelligence as AI designed to perform a specific bounded task. Fraud detection is narrow because it is optimized for one domain and purpose, unlike general intelligence. Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI)
Source
answer1: An AI system that detects fraudulent payment transactions in real time.
explanation1: This is ANI because the system is designed for one specific task: detecting fraud patterns in payments.
answer2: An AI system that can reason across any domain at human level.
explanation2: This describes a general intelligence capability, not a narrow task-specific system.
answer3: A digital agent with self-awareness and independent goals.
explanation3: Self-awareness is not a characteristic of ANI and suggests a speculative form of AI.
answer4: A model that autonomously invents new scientific theories across all disciplines.
explanation4: This implies broad general reasoning beyond the scope of ANI.

title: Does Chain-of-Thought prompting guarantee that an AI-generated answer is correct?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands both the usefulness and the limitation of Chain-of-Thought prompting. It may improve structure and inspectability, but human review remains necessary before relying on the response. Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
Source
answer1: No, it can support structured reasoning, but the output still requires human verification.
explanation1: Chain-of-Thought can make analysis more structured, but it does not eliminate errors, hallucinations, or weak assumptions.
answer2: Yes, because the model checks every reasoning step before answering.
explanation2: The model may appear to reason step by step, but that does not guarantee correctness.
answer3: Yes, because Chain-of-Thought permanently improves the model after each prompt.
explanation3: Prompting does not permanently retrain the underlying model.
answer4: No, because Chain-of-Thought prevents the model from performing analytical tasks.
explanation4: Chain-of-Thought is specifically used to support analytical tasks, even though outputs still need validation.

title: The Scrum Team's brainstorming session produces only familiar ideas. How can AI help most effectively?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master understands AI as a support for collaborative ideation, not as a replacement for team thinking. AI can help generate new angles, group related ideas, and surface patterns that the Scrum Team can then inspect together. brainstorm ideas, outline strategy, facilitate collaboration
Source
answer1: Use AI to generate alternative perspectives, cluster inputs, and reveal patterns for the team to inspect.
explanation1: AI can help expand thinking and organize ideas while the Scrum Team remains responsible for discussing and deciding what is useful.
answer2: Ask AI to select the best idea and start implementation immediately.
explanation2: AI should not replace team discussion or human decision-making during ideation.
answer3: Ask AI to create the final list so the team can skip brainstorming.
explanation3: Skipping human ideation weakens collaboration and shared ownership.
answer4: Stop the session until AI completes a full market analysis.
explanation4: A full market analysis may be excessive and does not directly support the team's immediate ideation challenge.

title: A Scrum Team faces the same integration issues across several Sprints without understanding the cause. How can AI help most effectively?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master can use AI to support empirical inspection without replacing the team's conversation. AI may help reveal repeated patterns, but the Scrum Team should discuss causes and adaptations together. AI-Enhanced Sprint Retrospective
Source
answer1: Use AI to surface recurring patterns for the team to discuss during the Sprint Retrospective.
explanation1: AI can help identify repeated signals, but the Scrum Team should inspect the patterns together and decide what to change.
answer2: Use AI to assign each recurring issue to the Developer most likely responsible.
explanation2: Attributing issues to individuals can damage trust and misses the systemic nature of many impediments.
answer3: Ask AI to automatically create action items and assign them before the Retrospective.
explanation3: Automatic assignment bypasses team discussion and weakens ownership of improvement actions.
answer4: Filter out repeated issues to keep the Retrospective focused on the current Sprint only.
explanation4: Filtering repeated issues hides valuable evidence that may reveal systemic problems.

title: A Scrum Master uses AI to identify themes from anonymous team survey responses before a Sprint Retrospective. What is most important?
feedback:
This question checks whether AI is used to support, not control, the Sprint Retrospective. AI-generated themes can help the Scrum Master prepare, but the team should be able to challenge, refine, or reject them. Keeping psychological safety high is a must.
Source
answer1: Share the AI-generated themes as a starting point the team can revise or reject.
explanation1: AI can support preparation, but the Scrum Team must retain ownership of the conversation and final agenda.
answer2: Present the AI-generated themes as the final retrospective agenda.
explanation2: This removes the team's ability to inspect and shape the discussion.
answer3: Use the same AI-generated theme structure for every Retrospective.
explanation3: A repeated structure may be useful sometimes, but each Retrospective should fit the team's current context.
answer4: Let AI decide which issues the team is ready to discuss.
explanation4: AI should not determine the team's readiness or replace facilitation judgment.

title: An AI assistant provides a polished market analysis, but several claims seem unsupported. What should the Scrum Team do next?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner recognizes that fluent AI output can still be factually wrong. Responsible use requires validating important claims against reliable sources before the information influences product decisions. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Verify the claims against trusted sources before using the analysis.
explanation1: A polished response can still contain false or unsupported claims, so verification is needed before relying on it.
answer2: Use the analysis because well-structured AI output is usually reliable.
explanation2: Good structure and writing quality do not prove factual accuracy.
answer3: Ask the AI whether its own claims are correct and accept the confirmation.
explanation3: The same AI may repeat or reinforce its own error, so independent validation is required.
answer4: Run the prompt several times and use the most common answer.
explanation4: Repeated outputs may still share the same hallucination or unsupported assumption.

title: Which statement best describes backpropagation in a neural network?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands backpropagation as a learning mechanism in neural networks. It adjusts internal weights so the model can reduce prediction error over training iterations. Backpropagation
Source
answer1: An algorithm that adjusts network weights using gradient-based updates.
explanation1: Backpropagation is used during training to reduce error by updating weights based on how much they contributed to the output error.
answer2: A method for compressing large datasets before model training.
explanation2: Compression reduces data size, but it does not describe how neural networks learn from errors.
answer3: A technique for storing long-term memory inside a Large Language Model.
explanation3: Backpropagation updates model parameters, it is not a memory storage mechanism.
answer4: A rule-based process for manually writing every decision path in the system.
explanation4: Backpropagation is not manual rule writing, it is an optimization process used in neural network training.

title: A Scrum Master wants the Scrum Team to explore AI without prescribing tools. What approach is most appropriate?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master supports empirical learning instead of prescribing AI practices. Small experiments allow the Scrum Team to inspect real outcomes and adapt based on usefulness, risks, and learning. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Encourage small AI experiments and inspect the outcomes together during the Sprint Retrospective.
explanation1: This helps the team learn empirically which AI uses are genuinely helpful without imposing practices prematurely.
answer2: Require every Developer to use the same AI tool in all Sprint work.
explanation2: Mandating one tool removes experimentation and may create adoption without learning.
answer3: Let the Scrum Master approve every AI experiment before the team tries it.
explanation3: This turns experimentation into control and weakens team ownership.
answer4: Adopt AI only after the organization defines a complete enterprise policy.
explanation4: Policy matters, but waiting for a complete policy can prevent safe, small learning experiments.

title: Developers often find that acceptance criteria are unclear during Product Backlog refinement. How can AI help most appropriately?
feedback:
This question checks whether AI is used as support for Product Backlog refinement rather than as a replacement for team collaboration. AI may help draft clearer criteria, but the Scrum Team should inspect and validate them together to build shared understanding. Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.
Source
answer1: Use AI to draft clearer acceptance criteria and validate them together as a Scrum Team.
explanation1: AI can help improve clarity, but the Scrum Team must inspect and validate whether the criteria reflect the product need.
answer2: Let AI finalize the acceptance criteria so refinement can be shortened.
explanation2: AI should not replace the Scrum Team's shared understanding during refinement.
answer3: Move vague items directly into the Sprint and let AI clarify them during development.
explanation3: Clarifying acceptance criteria too late can create misunderstanding and rework.
answer4: Create an AI Definition of Ready gate that automatically approves refined items.
explanation4: Automatic approval can weaken collaboration and create false confidence.

title: A Product Owner wants help preparing for Product Backlog refinement. How can AI best support this work?
feedback:
This question checks whether AI is used to support Product Backlog refinement rather than replace the people accountable for it. AI can help summarize feedback and draft clearer criteria, but the Scrum Team must inspect and validate the results. Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.
Source
answer1: Group stakeholder feedback, identify unclear Product Backlog items, and propose draft acceptance criteria.
explanation1: This uses AI to support preparation while keeping refinement collaborative and human-validated.
answer2: Automatically reorder the entire Product Backlog based on predicted market trends.
explanation2: AI may inform decisions, but Product Backlog ordering should not be fully automated without Product Owner accountability.
answer3: Assign story points to all Product Backlog items before the Developers review them.
explanation3: Story points or estimates should not be generated and locked by AI without Developer involvement.
answer4: Replace stakeholder conversations with AI-generated personas to save time.
explanation4: AI personas may support thinking, but they cannot replace real stakeholder feedback and collaboration.

title: A Scrum Master wants AI to draft a Sprint Goal using the team's established style. What is the most effective prompting approach?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands when few-shot prompting is more effective than a general instruction. When the team expects a specific format, examples of approved outputs help the model reproduce the desired pattern. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Provide a few examples of previously accepted Sprint Goals in the prompt.
explanation1: Examples help the model infer the expected structure, tone, and level of detail for the Sprint Goal.
answer2: Use zero-shot prompting with only a general definition of a Sprint Goal.
explanation2: A general definition may help, but it gives less guidance on the team's specific format.
answer3: Ask the AI to reason step by step before writing the Sprint Goal.
explanation3: Step-by-step reasoning may support analysis, but it does not best teach the expected output format.
answer4: Use retrieval-augmented generation to search for generic Sprint Goal templates.
explanation4: Generic templates may not match the team's agreed format.

title: What is the primary advantage of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for a large organization using LLMs?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands the core value of RAG. RAG helps an LLM produce grounded answers by retrieving relevant information before generating a response, without needing to retrain the model itself. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: It lets the model use relevant external or internal knowledge without retraining the core model.
explanation1: RAG can retrieve information from a knowledge source and provide it to the model at response time.
answer2: It allows the model to learn new tasks autonomously without human input.
explanation2: RAG retrieves information, it does not make the model autonomously learn tasks.
answer3: It reduces the size of the model by compressing knowledge into fewer parameters.
explanation3: RAG does not primarily compress model parameters, it adds retrieval to generation.
answer4: It eliminates the need for curated knowledge sources.
explanation4: RAG depends on useful, relevant, and maintained knowledge sources.

title: The Scrum Team uses AI to generate stakeholder reports, but the structure changes every time. What should they do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands how few-shot prompting improves format consistency. When the desired output has a specific structure, examples are more useful than general instructions alone. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Include a few examples of approved stakeholder reports in the prompt.
explanation1: Examples help the model recognize and reproduce the expected structure more consistently.
answer2: Accept the variability because LLM outputs are always unpredictable.
explanation2: LLMs can be guided toward more consistent outputs through better prompt design.
answer3: Use only zero-shot prompting to keep the model flexible.
explanation3: Zero-shot prompting gives less guidance when a specific format is expected.
answer4: Assign the model an expert role and rely on tone consistency.
explanation4: A role can help tone, but examples are stronger for demonstrating structure.

title: Developers increasingly ask AI to choose the technical approach instead of discussing options together. What is the main concern?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner recognizes that AI should support technical thinking without replacing the Scrum Team's shared judgment. When Developers stop discussing trade-offs together, self-management and shared accountability are weakened. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Delegating judgment to AI may reduce team self-management and shared accountability.
explanation1: The team risks treating AI as the decision-maker instead of using it as input for shared technical discussion.
answer2: The AI tool may not produce answers quickly enough during the Sprint.
explanation2: Speed is secondary to the risk of replacing team judgment and collaboration.
answer3: The Product Owner may disagree with the selected technical approach.
explanation3: The primary concern is the Developers' shared technical ownership, not Product Owner preference.
answer4: The AI tool may require additional licenses before full adoption.
explanation4: Licensing matters, but it is not the key Scrum concern in this situation.

title: A Scrum Team wants AI recommendations based on its actual Retrospective notes rather than generic agile advice. Which technique should be used?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands when RAG is more appropriate than other prompting techniques. When recommendations must be grounded in actual team artifacts, the AI needs access to those artifacts as retrieved context. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Use retrieval-augmented generation to supply the team's notes as context.
explanation1: RAG grounds the response in retrieved team-specific information instead of relying only on general model knowledge.
answer2: Use zero-shot prompting with a detailed description of the team's maturity level.
explanation2: A maturity description may help, but it does not ground the answer in the team's actual notes.
answer3: Use few-shot prompting with examples of retrospective formats.
explanation3: Few-shot examples can guide format, but they do not provide the team's real retrospective data.
answer4: Use Chain-of-Thought so the model reasons through general retrospective practices.
explanation4: Step-by-step reasoning may structure the answer, but it can still remain generic without the team's notes.

title: A large organization needs an AI assistant to answer questions using thousands of internal documents. Which approach is most appropriate?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands why RAG is useful for internal knowledge bases. RAG retrieves relevant documents at response time, allowing the AI to generate answers grounded in current organizational information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Use a RAG system that retrieves relevant indexed documents before generating an answer.
explanation1: RAG helps ground the answer in the organization's actual documents instead of relying only on the model's general training.
answer2: Rely on the LLM's pre-trained knowledge because it already contains broad information.
explanation2: Pre-trained knowledge is unlikely to include current or proprietary internal documents.
answer3: Retrain the model every day on all internal documents.
explanation3: Frequent retraining can be costly and still may not provide transparent source grounding.
answer4: Use keyword search only and avoid generated answers entirely.
explanation4: Keyword search can help retrieval, but it does not provide synthesized answers grounded in retrieved content.

title: A newly formed Scrum Team has no AI experience. What should the Scrum Master encourage first?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master introduces AI through empirical learning rather than pressure or avoidance. A small, low-risk experiment connected to a concrete need helps the team build capability and confidence while preserving inspection and adaptation. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Introduce one low-risk AI experiment tied to a real team need and debrief it in the Sprint Retrospective.
explanation1: This builds confidence through practical learning while allowing the team to inspect whether the AI use was helpful.
answer2: Require each Developer to learn AI tools individually before using them in Scrum activities.
explanation2: Individual homework may build isolated knowledge but does not create shared learning or team confidence.
answer3: Integrate AI into every Scrum event immediately to accelerate adoption.
explanation3: Broad adoption too early can overwhelm the team and create resistance or misuse.
answer4: Delay AI adoption until the team has mastered every Scrum practice.
explanation4: Waiting for full mastery can prevent safe learning from small, useful experiments.

title: A Scrum Team is preparing a complex proposal and wants to include multiple stakeholder viewpoints. Which prompting technique is most appropriate?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can prompt AI to broaden the analysis of a complex proposal. When multiple stakeholder viewpoints matter, the prompt should explicitly request different perspectives and contrasts instead of relying on a single persona or generic output. Generate multiple distinct possibilities
Source
answer1: Ask the AI to analyze the proposal from several stakeholder perspectives and include contrasting viewpoints.
explanation1: This helps the team avoid a single-angle answer and makes different concerns, risks, and expectations visible.
answer2: Use one expert persona to keep the tone and conclusions consistent.
explanation2: A single persona may improve consistency, but it can narrow the range of perspectives.
answer3: Use zero-shot prompting and let the model decide which viewpoints matter.
explanation3: Zero-shot prompting may miss important perspectives if they are not explicitly requested.
answer4: Use RAG only to ground the proposal in factual data.
explanation4: RAG can support factual grounding, but it does not by itself ensure contrasting stakeholder perspectives.

title: Scrum Team members generate user stories with different AI prompts and inconsistent formats. What should the Scrum Master encourage?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that inconsistent AI output can often be improved through shared prompt design. A common template helps the Scrum Team align on structure, persona, and criteria without removing team ownership. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Establish a shared prompt template defining the expected format, persona, and acceptance criteria guidance.
explanation1: A shared template gives the team a repeatable structure while preserving collaboration and consistent output quality.
answer2: Require one person to write all AI prompts for the whole team.
explanation2: Centralizing all prompting reduces shared capability and creates dependency on one person.
answer3: Choose the best AI-generated user story each Sprint and copy its style afterward.
explanation3: Copying one output is less reliable than defining a reusable prompt template.
answer4: Accept all format differences because self-managing teams should use their own styles.
explanation4: Self-management does not mean ignoring inconsistency that harms shared understanding.

title: A Scrum Master receives an AI-generated impediment removal plan, but one action may conflict with company policy. What should the Scrum Master do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master treats AI output as decision support rather than authority. A well-reasoned AI plan may still include recommendations that conflict with organizational policy, so specific validation is required before use. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Validate the specific action against current policy before using it.
explanation1: AI-generated reasoning may be useful, but any recommendation that could conflict with policy must be checked before inclusion.
answer2: Ask the AI to confirm whether the action complies with company policy.
explanation2: The same AI may not have current or authoritative policy context, so independent validation is needed.
answer3: Use the full plan because the AI explained its reasoning step by step.
explanation3: Step-by-step reasoning does not guarantee that the recommendation is compliant or safe.
answer4: Discard the entire plan because one recommendation may be risky.
explanation4: A single risky recommendation should be validated or removed, not automatically invalidate the whole plan.

title: After several Sprints using AI-generated refinement summaries, Developers feel less connected to the Product Backlog. What should the Scrum Master do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master can inspect the human impact of AI use rather than focusing only on efficiency. AI-generated summaries may help preparation, but if they disconnect Developers from the Product Backlog, the practice should be adapted. The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.
Source
answer1: Inspect how AI is being used and adapt the practice to restore meaningful team engagement.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should help the Scrum Team examine whether the AI practice supports or weakens shared understanding of the Product Backlog.
answer2: Increase the number of refinement sessions to compensate for the AI summaries.
explanation2: More sessions do not solve the underlying problem if the AI practice is reducing engagement.
answer3: Continue using the summaries because they save time during refinement.
explanation3: Time savings are not valuable if the team loses understanding and ownership of the Product Backlog.
answer4: Ask the Product Owner to take full responsibility for backlog engagement.
explanation4: The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, but refinement and understanding involve the Scrum Team.

title: An AI assistant proposes automatically changing the company's refund policy without consulting stakeholders. What is the most responsible action?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners understand that AI-generated policy changes require human accountability, stakeholder consultation, and responsible governance. AI can assist by proposing options, but it should not autonomously implement changes that may affect customers, trust, compliance, or organizational commitments. Avoid (AI stays out, humans decide and act)
Source
answer1: Treat the proposal as a suggestion and require human review with stakeholder input before implementation.
explanation1: AI can support policy analysis, but changes that affect customers and stakeholders require accountable human review before implementation.
answer2: Deploy the change if the AI reports a high confidence score.
explanation2: A confidence score does not replace stakeholder consultation or human accountability.
answer3: Remove traceability from the proposal to simplify approval.
explanation3: Removing traceability weakens transparency and accountability.
answer4: Let the AI manage future refund policy updates autonomously.
explanation4: Policy changes with stakeholder impact should not be delegated fully to AI.
